- A **linear regulator**, like the classic 7805, is simple, cheap and electrically quiet. But it burns off the extra voltage as heat. The heat it makes, in watts, is: (voltage in − voltage out) × current in amps.
- A **switching regulator**, often called a **buck converter**, switches the power on and off very fast and smooths it out. It usually wastes only 5 to 15% of the power and stays cool, so it is the better choice for big drops or big currents.

There is a second reason to give the brain its own steady supply. When motors start or get stuck, they pull a big current, and the battery voltage dips for a moment. A brain on the same wire can reset in the middle of a run. This is called a **brownout**. A regulator, capacitors, or even a separate battery for the brain keep its power steady.
lessons.task: A 7805 linear regulator turns a 12 V battery into 5 V for a board that draws 0.5 A. How much power does the regulator turn into heat? Answer in **watts (W)**.
lessons.hint: Find how many volts the regulator has to drop, then multiply by the current in amps.

check.explain: Voltage dropped: 12 V − 5 V = 7 V. Heat: 7 V × 0.5 A = **3.5 W**. That is more heat than the board itself uses (5 V × 0.5 A = 2.5 W), enough to make a small regulator too hot to touch or make it shut down without a big heatsink. A buck converter at about 90% efficiency would waste only about 0.3 W.

lessons.title: Tidy Wires and Fuses
lessons.goal: Wire a robot neatly and choose and place a fuse correctly.
lessons.theory:
Most robot faults are wiring faults: a wire pulled loose by a wheel, or a **short circuit**, where bare metal on the positive side touches the negative side. A short on a lithium battery can push tens of amps or more through a wire, make it glow hot, and start a fire.

Good habits:

- Red for positive, black for negative (ground). Always.
- Thick wire for motor power, thin wire only for signals.
- Tie wires down, keep them away from wheels and moving joints, and leave a little slack where parts move.
- Cover bare metal with heat-shrink tubing.
- Use connectors that only fit one way round, so a battery cannot be plugged in backwards.
- Add a main power switch you can reach easily.

A **fuse** is a thin strip of metal that melts and breaks the circuit when the current gets too high. Two rules make it work:

- **Rating:** a bit above the most current the robot normally draws, so it does not blow in normal use, but below what the wire can safely carry, so it blows before the wire overheats.
- **Position:** in the positive wire, as close to the battery as possible, so it protects all the wire after it.

If a fuse blows, find out why before you replace it. Never put in a bigger fuse, or a piece of wire, just to make the problem go away.
lessons.task: Your robot draws at most 3.5 A, even when the motors start. Its main power wire can carry 10 A safely. Which fuse, in which place, is right?
lessons.hint: Check both rules: the rating must sit between normal current and the wire's limit, and the position must protect the whole wire.

options: A 2 A fuse, next to the motors
A 5 A fuse in the positive wire, right next to the battery
A 30 A fuse in the positive wire, right next to the battery, so it never blows by mistake
A 5 A fuse in the positive wire, at the far end next to the motor driver
why: 2 A is below the 3.5 A the robot normally draws, so it would blow every time the motors start. And next to the motors, it leaves the wire from the battery unprotected.
Right. 5 A is above the 3.5 A the robot normally needs and below the 10 A the wire can carry, and next to the battery it protects the whole wire.
The wire can only carry 10 A safely. A 30 A fuse would let the wire overheat long before the fuse melts, so it protects nothing.
The rating is right, but a short circuit anywhere between the battery and the fuse would bypass it. The fuse belongs next to the battery.
check.explain: 5 A sits between the robot's normal 3.5 A and the wire's 10 A limit, and placing it right at the battery's positive terminal protects every bit of wire after it.

lessons.title: A Common Ground
lessons.goal: Explain why parts that share signals must share a ground.
lessons.theory:
Voltage is always measured **between two points**, a bit like height is measured from the floor. In a circuit, that floor is called **ground**: GND on the pin labels, 0 V, the negative side of the battery.

When an Arduino sends a 5 V "go" signal to a motor driver, the driver checks one thing: is this signal wire 5 V above **my** ground? That works fine when both boards run from the same battery, because they stand on the same floor.

Many robots use two batteries: one for the motors and one for the brain. Then there are two separate floors. If their grounds are not connected, the driver has nothing to measure the signal against. It may ignore the signal, or react to it at random.

The rule: every part that exchanges signals must share a **common ground**. Connect the GND of the brain, the motor driver and the sensors together.

Two warnings:

- Join the **grounds** only. Never connect the positive wires of two different batteries together.
- Never feed a higher voltage into a pin made for a lower one.

Typical signs of a missing ground: motors that twitch for no reason, sensor readings that jump around, or a robot that only works when you touch it. When you see these, check the ground wire before you blame a part.
lessons.task: An Arduino runs from a USB power bank. Its motor driver runs from a separate 7.4 V battery. Signal wires go from the Arduino's pins to the driver's inputs, but the motors twitch at random or ignore commands. What should you do first?
lessons.hint: The two boards run from different batteries. What must they share for signals to make sense?

options: Connect the Arduino's GND to the motor driver's GND
Connect the 7.4 V battery's positive wire to the Arduino's 5 V pin, so both boards share power
Use longer signal wires, so the signal becomes stronger
Replace the motor driver, because it must be broken
why: Right. With the grounds joined, both boards measure voltage from the same floor, so the driver can read the Arduino's signals.
Never join the positives of two batteries, and never put 7.4 V into a 5 V pin: that can destroy the Arduino. Only the grounds should be joined.
A longer wire does not make a signal stronger. The problem is that the driver has no shared ground to measure the signal against.
Random twitching with two separate batteries is the classic sign of a missing ground. Check the wiring before you blame a part.
check.explain: Signals are voltages measured from ground. Joining the grounds gives both boards the same reference, so the driver reads the Arduino's commands correctly.

lessons.title: Charging and Lithium Care
lessons.goal: Charge, store and handle lithium batteries safely.
lessons.theory:
Lithium batteries (LiPo and Li-ion) pack a lot of energy into very little weight. That is why robots and drones use them, and it is also why they must be treated with respect. A damaged or misused lithium battery can swell, get very hot and catch fire.

Charging:

- Use only a charger made for that battery type and cell count. For LiPo packs, use a **balance charger** with the balance plug connected, so every cell ends at the same voltage, never above 4.2 V.
- Charge on a non-flammable surface or in a LiPo safety bag, and never leave it charging unattended.
- Let a hot battery cool down before you charge it.

Using and storing:

- Do not drain it too far. Never let a cell drop below about 3.0 V; many people stop at 3.3 V to make the pack last longer. A cheap low-voltage alarm warns you.
- For storage longer than a few days, leave the cells at about 3.8 V (many chargers have a "storage" mode), somewhere cool and dry.
- Cover the terminals so they can never short.

Warning signs: a pack that is **puffy** (swollen), dented, punctured or hot for no reason is damaged. Stop using it, do not charge it, keep it away from anything that burns, and take it to a battery recycling point. Never put it in the household bin.

The Power, Batteries and Charging course covers charging in depth.
lessons.task: After a crash, you notice your robot's LiPo pack has become slightly puffy, although it still powers the robot. What should you do?
lessons.hint: A puffy pack is one of the warning signs in the briefing. What does the briefing say to do with a damaged pack?

options: Charge it fully, so the cells can recover their shape
Keep using it, but only at half speed to go easy on it
Press it flat and wrap it tightly in tape
Stop using it: do not charge it, keep it away from anything that burns, and take it to a battery recycling point
why: Charging a damaged lithium pack is one of the most likely ways to start a fire. Swelling does not go away.
A swollen pack is damaged inside. Using it gently does not repair it, and it can still overheat and catch fire.
Pressing on a damaged cell can cause a short circuit inside it, which can start a fire.
Right. Swelling means the pack is damaged inside. The safe move is to stop using and charging it, store it where a fire could not spread, and recycle it properly.
check.explain: A puffy LiPo is damaged, and charging or using it can start a fire. Retire it safely: no charging, nothing flammable nearby, and off to battery recycling.

lessons.title: Choose Your First Project
lessons.goal: Compare the two classic first robots and match each to its sensors.
lessons.theory:
Two projects are the classic first robots, and both are great.

A **line follower** drives along a dark line on a light floor. Two or more **IR reflectance sensors** sit under the front, pointing down. Each one shines invisible infrared light at the floor and measures how much bounces back: the light floor reflects a lot, the dark line very little. The brain steers to keep the line between the sensors. This project teaches sensing and the control loop, and later PID, for fast and smooth following.

An **obstacle avoider** drives around a room and turns away before it hits things. It uses a forward-facing distance sensor. An **ultrasonic sensor** sends out a short burst of sound, too high for you to hear, and times the echo; a common one measures from about 2 cm to 4 m. Some avoiders use IR distance sensors instead. This project teaches distance sensing and simple state machines: driving, turning, driving again.

Both robots share the same base:

- a chassis with two driven wheels and a free-rolling caster wheel
- two DC gear motors and a motor driver
- a microcontroller brain
- a battery with a switch and a fuse

Pick the project that fits your space. A line follower needs a track, which can be black electrical tape on a light floor. An obstacle avoider needs a room with walls and boxes. Start simple, make it work, then improve it.
lessons.task: You want your first robot to race around a track made of black electrical tape on a white floor. Which project and sensors match?
lessons.hint: The tape is flat on the floor. Which sensor tells dark from light, rather than near from far?

options: An obstacle avoider with an ultrasonic sensor facing forward
A line follower with an ultrasonic sensor pointing down at the floor
A line follower with IR reflectance sensors pointing down at the floor
A line follower with a camera, run by an Arduino Uno
why: An ultrasonic sensor sees walls and boxes in front of the robot. Flat tape on the floor gives it nothing to detect.
An ultrasonic sensor measures distance. The tape and the floor are at the same distance, so it cannot tell them apart.
Right. IR reflectance sensors see the difference between light floor and dark tape, which is exactly what a line follower needs.
An Arduino Uno does not have nearly enough memory to handle camera images. Simple IR sensors do this job far more easily.
check.explain: A tape track calls for a line follower, and IR reflectance sensors pointing at the floor tell the dark tape from the light floor.

lessons.title: Picking the Parts
lessons.goal: Check a parts list against the job, part by part.
lessons.theory:
A parts list is where many first robots go wrong, before a single wire is connected. Go through it part by part and ask two questions: what does this part do, and do its numbers match the rest of the robot?

- **Brain:** a microcontroller for simple sensors and motors; a single-board computer only if you need a camera or heavy computing.
- **Motor driver:** a brain's pin can only give a tiny current (about 20 mA on an Arduino Uno), but a motor needs hundreds of milliamps or more. The motor driver handles that big current for the brain. Its current rating, per motor, must be above the most current a motor can draw, which is its **stall current**: the current it pulls when it is stuck and cannot turn.
- **Motors:** their rated voltage should be close to the battery voltage.
- **Sensors:** the right kind for the job, as in the last mission.
- **Power:** a battery that suits the motors, a regulator to give the brain its steady 5 V, a switch and a fuse.

Stall current matters because a motor stalls every time it starts from rest, and whenever it gets stuck against a wall. A driver rated below that current overheats or shuts itself down, often in the middle of a run.

Tick each part off against the job and against the other parts, and write the key numbers next to it.
lessons.task: You are building an obstacle avoider. Its motors are rated for 7.2 V, and each one can draw up to 1.5 A when stalled. Which parts list will work?
lessons.hint: Check each list for one number that does not match: pin current, pin voltage or driver rating.

options: Arduino Uno with the motors wired straight to its pins, a forward-facing ultrasonic sensor, and a 7.2 V NiMH pack with a switch and a fuse
Raspberry Pi, a motor driver rated 2 A per motor, a forward-facing ultrasonic sensor, and a 7.2 V NiMH pack wired straight to the Pi's 5 V pin, with a switch and a fuse
Arduino Uno, a motor driver rated 0.5 A per motor, a forward-facing ultrasonic sensor, and a 7.2 V NiMH pack with a switch, a fuse and a 5 V regulator for the Arduino
Arduino Uno, a motor driver rated 2 A per motor, a forward-facing ultrasonic sensor, and a 7.2 V NiMH pack with a switch, a fuse and a 5 V regulator for the Arduino
why: An Arduino pin gives only about 20 mA, but each motor can draw up to 1.5 A. The robot needs a motor driver between the brain and the motors.
7.2 V straight into a 5 V pin can destroy the Pi. It needs a regulator. A Pi is also more brain than an obstacle avoider needs.
0.5 A is far below the motors' 1.5 A stall current, so the driver would overheat or shut down every time the motors start or get stuck.
Right. The driver's 2 A is above the 1.5 A stall current, the pack matches the 7.2 V motors, and the regulator gives the Arduino a steady 5 V.
check.explain: Every number matches: the 2 A driver covers the motors' 1.5 A stall current, the 7.2 V pack suits the 7.2 V motors, and the regulator keeps the Arduino on a steady 5 V.

lessons.title: Build in the Right Order
lessons.goal: Put the steps of a robot build in an order where each step can be checked before the next.
lessons.theory:
Build your robot in an order where every step can be checked before the next one hides it. Then, when something fails, only the newest step can be to blame.

A good order:

- **Plan:** sketch the robot, draw a wiring diagram and write the parts list.
- **Chassis:** mount the motors, wheels and caster.
- **Power:** add the battery, switch, fuse and regulator. Measure the voltages with a multimeter before connecting anything else.
- **Brain:** connect it and load a tiny test program, like blinking an LED.
- **Motors:** connect the motor driver and test each motor on its own.
- **Sensors:** add them one at a time and check that their readings make sense.
- **Behaviour:** only now write the full program, with its control loop and states.
- **Tune:** test on the real track or in the real room, and improve.

Two habits help at every stage. Disconnect the battery while you change any wiring. And after each step, switch on and check that everything that worked before still works.

You can sketch your program early, and that is fine. But you cannot really test it until the hardware under it has been proven. If you try, bugs in the program and faults in the wiring get tangled together, and you cannot tell which is which.
lessons.task:
A friend has four build steps written on cards:

```text
P. Write the full robot program
Q. Test each motor on its own
R. Wire the battery, switch and fuse, and measure the voltages
S. Mount the motors and wheels on the chassis
```

In which order should they do them?
lessons.hint: Each step should be testable using only the steps done before it. What does a motor test need to exist first?

options: S, R, Q, P
P, S, R, Q
R, S, P, Q
S, Q, R, P
why: Right. First the chassis, then proven power, then each motor tested, and only then the full program on hardware you trust.
You can sketch code early, but you cannot test the full program until the motors and power are proven. Bugs and wiring faults would get tangled together.
Wiring the power before the chassis leaves loose parts and live wires to work around, and writing the program before the motors are tested mixes program bugs with wiring faults.
You cannot test a motor before the battery, switch and fuse are wired: it would have no power.
check.explain: Chassis, then power, then a test of each motor, then the full program. Each step is checked using only what was built before it.

lessons.title: Test One Part at a Time
lessons.goal: Test parts separately and use your measurements to predict runtime.
lessons.theory:
Before you run the whole robot, give every part its own small test.

- **Motors:** does each wheel turn the right way, at slow and fast speeds?
- **Sensors:** show the readings while you move your hand or the line under the sensor. Write down typical numbers, like the reading over the floor and the reading over the tape.
- **E-stop and switch:** do they really cut the power?

Keep notes as you go. When a part passes, you know it works. When the whole robot later misbehaves, you can go back to the last thing that worked.

While you test, measure how much **current** each part draws. You can use a multimeter set to measure current, or a small power meter between the battery and the robot. Your notes then become a **power budget**:

- Add the currents of all the parts that run at the same time to get the total.
- Check that the total is below what your fuse, regulator and motor driver can handle.
- Use the total to predict the runtime with the formula from Power and Wiring: (capacity × 0.8) ÷ total current.

Measured numbers beat guesses from a product page. Real motors on a real chassis often draw more than the label says, because of friction, the weight of the robot and the floor.
lessons.task:
Your test notes, for everything running at once:

```text
Arduino and sensors   60 mA
Motor driver          40 mA
Left motor, driving  380 mA
Right motor, driving 380 mA
```

The battery is 2000 mAh, and you plan to use only 80% of it. How long can the robot drive? Answer in **minutes**, rounded to the nearest whole minute.
lessons.hint: Add up all four currents first, then use the runtime formula with the 80% margin, and turn hours into minutes.

check.explain: Total current: 60 + 40 + 380 + 380 = 860 mA. Usable capacity: 2000 mAh × 0.8 = 1600 mAh. Runtime: 1600 ÷ 860 = 1.86 hours. In minutes: 1.86 × 60 = 111.6, which rounds to **112 min**.

lessons.title: Debugging a Misbehaving Robot
lessons.goal: Find the most likely cause of a robot fault from what you observe.
lessons.theory:
Every builder's first robot misbehaves. Debugging is detective work:

- Describe exactly what you see, not what you think is wrong.
- List the likely causes, and check the easiest and most likely one first.
- Change **one** thing at a time, then test again.

Some common symptoms and their usual causes:

- **Spins on the spot** instead of driving straight: one wheel turns backwards. Most often, that motor's two wires are swapped at the driver. Swap them back, or reverse that motor's direction in the program.
- **Drives in a wide curve:** one wheel is slower. Real motors are never identical, and a wheel may be rubbing. Closed-loop control with wheel encoders fixes this properly.
- **Ignores obstacles:** first show the sensor readings while you move your hand in front of it. If they do not change, look for a loose or swapped wire, a missing common ground, or a sensor that faces the wrong way. If the readings are fine, look at the program: a slow loop, or a long wait, leaves the robot blind.
- **Resets when the motors start:** a brownout. Give the brain a steadier supply.

A quick trick for motor problems: lift the robot so its wheels spin freely in the air, and watch each wheel while you command it.
lessons.task: You press start. Your robot should drive straight ahead, but it spins on the spot. You lift it and command "both motors forward": the left wheel turns forward and the right wheel turns backward, both at the same speed. What is the most likely cause?
lessons.hint: The two wheels turn at the same speed but in opposite directions. What makes only one of them turn the wrong way?

options: The battery is nearly empty
The right motor's two wires are swapped at the motor driver
The ultrasonic sensor is facing the wrong way
The control loop is running too slowly
why: A weak battery would make both wheels slower. It would not make one of them turn backward.
Right. Swapped wires make a DC motor turn the other way. Swap that motor's two wires at the driver, or reverse its direction in the program.
Here you commanded both motors directly, with no sensor involved, and one wheel still turned the wrong way. The sensor cannot cause this.
A slow loop reacts late, but you gave a direct command and one wheel turned the wrong way. That is a wiring or direction problem, not a timing one.
check.explain: When one wheel turns backward to a forward command, that motor's two wires are almost always swapped. Swap them at the driver, or reverse that motor in the program.

lessons.title: Capstone: The Design Review
lessons.goal: Combine ideas from the whole course to judge a complete robot design, and see where to go next.
lessons.theory:
You now know what a robot is made of: body, senses, muscles, brain, power and wiring. Here is where the academy's Python courses take each idea further:

- **Python for Robotics:** write real control loops, read sensors and build a robot simulator.
- **Control Theory and PID:** build and tune your own PID controller.
- **Kinematics and Dynamics:** the maths of how arms and wheeled robots move.
- **Computer Vision for Robots:** teach a robot to see with a camera.
- **Path Planning and Navigation:** find a route through a map.
- **ROS 2, the Robot Nervous System:** the software that connects the parts of big robots.
- **Aerial Robots:** drones.
- **Power, Batteries and Charging** and **Embedded Linux for Robots:** go deeper into batteries and into Linux boards like the Raspberry Pi.

Before that, one last mission. Engineers hold a **design review**: before anyone builds, the team reads the plan and looks for the part that will fail. You will do the same now. Check each plan against what you have learned:

- Is the brain right for the work it must do?
- Does the robot use feedback where it needs to be accurate?
- Do all parts that share signals share a ground?
- Does the emergency stop work even if the program freezes?
lessons.task: A team wants a robot that follows a person around the school hall using a camera. All four plans share wheel motors with encoders, a motor driver, a 3000 mAh battery, a fuse next to the battery, and a regulator that gives the brains a steady 5 V. At an average draw of 1.5 A, using 80% of the battery, every plan expects about 96 minutes of driving. Which plan passes the design review?
lessons.hint: Check each plan against the four questions in the briefing. Only one passes all four.

options: An Arduino Uno finds the person in the camera image and runs a closed loop on the wheels using the encoders. All grounds are joined. A latching e-stop cuts motor power.

A Raspberry Pi finds the person in the camera image and sends speed orders to a microcontroller, which runs a closed loop on the wheels. All grounds are joined. The e-stop is a key on a laptop that tells the program to stop the motors.
A Raspberry Pi finds the person in the camera image and sends speed orders to a microcontroller, which runs a closed loop on the wheels. All grounds are joined. A latching e-stop cuts motor power.

A Raspberry Pi finds the person in the camera image and sends speed orders to a microcontroller, which runs a closed loop on the wheels. The motor battery's ground is kept apart from the brains' ground, to avoid noise. A latching e-stop cuts motor power.
why: An Arduino Uno has only 2 KB of working memory, far too little to hold and search a camera image. Vision needs a single-board computer.
An e-stop that asks the program to stop does nothing if the program has frozen. It must cut the motor power in the wiring.
Right. The Pi does the vision, the microcontroller keeps the wheels on target with feedback, the shared ground lets their signals work, and the e-stop works even if the software freezes.
Without a common ground, the motor driver has nothing to measure the microcontroller's signals against, so the motors twitch or ignore commands.
check.explain: This plan puts each job on the right brain, uses feedback on the wheels, shares one ground, and has an e-stop that cuts motor power in the wiring. The runtime checks out too: 3000 mAh × 0.8 = 2400 mAh, and 2400 ÷ 1500 mA = 1.6 hours = 96 minutes.
